en: Volume Four, Part One, composed by Li Tongxuan of the Great Tang at Beiping.
Regarding the Ten Stages: from this point onward, the nine night goddesses and the one Gopā are [the subjects].
In the past, during his causal stage, the Tathāgata was once their husband and wife; now that he has perfected the Way, he serves as their spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) on the tenth stage.
As the text of the following sutra itself contains, this will become clear once one reaches that position.

From this point forward, there are ten spiritual friends for each stage of the ten bhūmis and the stage of Equal Enlightenment; collectively, these rely on the fulfillment of practice and vows within the ten dedications, which constitutes their method.

The two stages of Equality and Wondrousness constitute the fulfillment of Samantabhadra’s practice; this is because they represent the completion of the practice of dedication through the fulfillment of dharma-vows.

This extends from the fruits of what is believed within the ten levels of faith, up to the fundamental Wisdom of Universal Radiance attained within the ten abodes, which is the full accomplishment of the fruit of practice. This is because the wisdom is one and the same throughout the preceding and succeeding stages.
This merely clarifies that the modes of cultivation differ between the raw and the matured; it does not imply a distinction in the wisdom itself.
In the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is primary, while the other nine serve as its companions.

Regarding this land of Magadha in Jambudvīpa, the reason it is not referred to as "the south" is that this country is the place where the Buddha was born; by meeting his original essence, it symbolizes that his fundamental wisdom is not limited by direction, thereby clarifying his perfect, all-encompassing wisdom.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they encompass the subsequent two positions of Equality (*samatā*) and Subtlety (*pranīta*).

Having reached fulfillment, one proceeds through the intermediate stages of the Middle Way, wherein wisdom and compassion ascend and arise; for in this position, wisdom, vision, vows, and practice are cultivated with shared aspiration.

Thereafter, one establishes the sequence of maturation and ripening through the cultivation of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), ensuring that one may emerge from the mundane world yet remain within the entanglements of saṃsāra, thereby perfecting both wisdom and compassion.

The realization of the fruits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the two supreme awakenings (*abhisambodhi*) arises collectively from the initial stages of the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the ten stages; for each of these initially encompasses all subsequent positions, as the vows and practices are simultaneously initiated to bring about the later stages.
If there were no beginning, how could there be any subsequent dharma that could be practiced?
It is only through the initial mind that the subsequent stages are established.
Just as with a hundred-fathom tiered terrace, if its construction lacks even a single measure of earth, the final result cannot be achieved because the fruit lacks its initial cause.
It is like a seed sowing a fruit: only after the cause has arisen can the fruit subsequently exist, for it is not different from the initial cause and fruit.
By this, the initial resolve of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) encompasses all subsequent stages; both time and wisdom are entirely included within it, without the slightest difference.

However, having separately opened up the stages of ascending progress and maturation, at the very beginning of the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), when one first initiates the resolve for enlightenment, one is still similar to ordinary beings, taking the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) as the foremost.

The second stage, the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*), takes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) as its primary focus; therein, one finally abandons wife and children, leaves the household life for homelessness, cultivates the essence of the precepts, purifies that which is clung to, and subdues the afflictions of the desire realm.

In the third stage, the Radiant (*Prabhākari*), one cultivates the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the higher form realm and the formless realm, remedies the afflictions associated with delighting in tranquility, and attains the manifestation of karma pertaining to the three realms.

Having already transcended the three realms with a mind predominant in the higher stages, one reaches the fourth stage, the Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*). Here, one cultivates the contemplation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) by observing the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena (*kāya-vedanā-citta-dharma*).

Within the sphere of mind and objects, one transforms all worldly dharmas to become clear and pure; thus, regarding all activities within the three realms, the mind becomes unattached and is born into the family of the Tathāgata.

The fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjaya), employs meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to treat the two truths of suffering and its origin among the Four Noble Truths. It realizes that the fundamental nature of worldly afflictions is inherently pure, being nothing other than cessation and the path; it clarifies that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself liberation and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This serves to counteract the obstacles of those of the Śrāvaka vehicle and of Bodhisattvas in Pure Lands who fear suffering, seek personal nirvana, and—due to a lack of wisdom and compassion—abandon sentient beings.

The sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), involves the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination. One contemplates that the six sense faculties and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) apprehending objects are termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

By contemplating that the six sense faculties and name-and-form are fundamentally empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, one becomes free from the five views—such as those of internal, external, middle, or extremes—and this constitutes the sovereign, wondrous function of the activity of wisdom (*jñānakarma*). Thus, one immediately accomplishes the divine power of immeasurable wisdom and liberation.
By eliminating the contemplation of the pratyekabuddhas regarding the twelve links of dependent origination and taking emptiness as their realization, they lack the wisdom for liberation.
Abandoning the obstacles to great compassion, they give rise to immeasurable wisdom and supernormal powers to transform and teach sentient beings.
Through the accomplishment of the three aforementioned stages, one attains supramundane wisdom within the mundane world.
Through the six perfections mentioned above, one completes the single cycle of liberation, both supramundane and mundane-within-supramundane.

The seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (*dūraṃgamā*), enters into birth and death, harmonizing and fusing the defiled and the pure; it perfects great compassion, does not abandon the realm of sentient beings in the world, and brings to gradual fulfillment the subsequent non-effortful wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*).

Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s stage of wondrous enlightenment is accomplished on this basis; by removing the obstacle of lack of mastery within birth and death, it causes the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four kinds of unimpeded eloquence, great wisdom, and great compassion to be fully perfected and sovereign. Thus, he dwells perpetually within birth and death, seeking nothing else as a separate transcendence from the world.

The eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), is the perfection of effortlessness (*anābhoga-jñāna*). It is not separate from what was accomplished in the seventh stage; at the conclusion of this stage, compassion becomes effortless within the midst of birth and death, and pure wisdom manifests before one, as seen in the assembly where Avalokiteśvara and Samantagāmin meet.

From this point on, there is no further progress to be known; however, by means of the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas, one is enabled to recollect original vows and give rise to compassion for the benefit of sentient beings.
Because pure wisdom is so vast, the arising of compassion in a single thought-moment is such that the merit of Bodhisattvas on the lower stages cannot equal it.
The three augmentations are: first, the Tathāgata manifests his body; second, he touches [the disciple’s] head with his hand; third, he praises them through the activity of speech.
The seven exhortations are: first, exhorting the cultivation of the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and eighteen unique qualities;
second, exhorting the practice of diligence and not abandoning the gate of the patience of non-arising.
Third, they are exhorted to have compassion for all sentient beings;
fourth, they are exhorted to recollect their original vows to benefit all sentient beings;
fifth, they are exhorted to cultivate the physical marks of the Buddhas, their buddha-fields, and their karmic rewards.
Sixth, they exhort the study of the immeasurable Dharma-gates of the Buddha;
seventh, they exhort the study of the wisdom regarding the diverse karmas of immeasurable sentient beings.
They fully master these to give rise to the karma of compassion and wisdom, ensuring that one does not become stalled in the gateway of effortless wisdom.
In all the preceding stages, one has cultivated liberation through craving and harmonized wisdom with compassion.

Upon reaching this stage, having fully perfected the great wisdom and compassion that reconcile and liberate within the ocean of birth and death, one then studies the functional power of the Buddha’s great liberation.
Therefore, through three additions and seven exhortations, one is caused to advance and not remain stagnant within the wisdom of non-attainment.
In the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*), one attains unimpeded eloquence and enters the rank of a Dharma Master.

The four unhindered dharmas are: first, the unhindered knowledge of phenomena; second, the unhindered knowledge of meaning; third, the unhindered knowledge of language; and fourth, the unhindered knowledge of eloquence.

The tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi), is equal to the rank of a Buddha in its fullness; one receives the office of a Tathāgata and sits upon a single great Lotus King-throne, whose dimensions are equal to ten million billion trichiliocosms.
In the three vehicles, from the first stage up to the tenth bhūmi, the size of the seat is equal to one trichiliocosm.

In this One Vehicle, when the path of the ten bhūmis is perfected, it is not merely that one sits upon a flower-king throne as vast as a million trichiliocosms; there are also lotus thrones as numerous as the atoms within thirteen thousand great thousand-world systems serving as its retinue, with immeasurable bodhisattvas each sitting upon the remaining lotuses surrounding it on all sides.
These ten stages of the Dharma are all studied simultaneously within the first stage.

For this reason, within the body of this Night Goddess, she contains the realms of all sentient beings; even within the pores of her skin, she contains the constellations, the sun and moon, and the realms of all sentient beings.
The dwelling place of this spiritual friend is simply called the land of Jambudvīpa, rather than being specified as the south.
The city named Kapilavastu means "Great Essence" (Mahātman) in this language.
Among the five regions of India, this country has its capital at the city of Ayodhyā; because it encompasses all other nations, it is called "The Great Entity" (Mahāśarīra).
It is also called the City of Yellow Objects (Pītadravya), as it was so named after having been the dwelling place of the Yellow-headed Rishi (Pītaśiras) in ancient times.

Furthermore, it is situated in the central region among the five parts of India, encompassing all surrounding countries; because its geomantic configuration is like the central palace of the *wusi* (earth) element, circular and pervasive, it is called the City of Yellow Objects.
That Sudhana enters through the eastern gate of the city signifies his initial entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*) among the ten stages.
"East" refers to the wisdom that awakens and initiates illumination for sentient beings; therefore, he enters through the eastern gate of the city.

Standing for no long time before seeing the sun rise means that, from the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) onward, when one contemplates and seeks to advance toward the dharma-gate corresponding to this stage, it is called "entering the city."
To harmonize with and integrate the fruit of this stage is called "not long after standing.
Because the obstacles of the preceding stage have vanished and the wisdom of this stage has manifested, it is called "the rising of the sun.
Furthermore, because one enters the long night of birth and death to preach the Dharma and transform sentient beings, it is called "the celestial deity."

Then he beheld the night goddess in the void, dwelling within a precious pavilion; having realized the emptiness of all phenomena through the practice of great compassion, she had given rise to immeasurable gateways of wisdom, which were the fruits born of her retribution.

Regarding those who sit upon the fragrant lotus-treasury lion throne: this is to clarify that the bodhisattvas of the ten stages and above cultivate the practice of great compassion; thus, the night goddesses and the lotus seats are employed as symbols to represent this.

"Incense" clarifies fundamental wisdom; it refers to the fragrance of the fivefold dharma-body—consisting of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—which is fully perfected. It takes the practice of nurturing great kindness and great compassion as its essential seat.
This can be understood by contemplating it through its imagery.
Here, nine night goddesses and one Gopā are all female figures, which clarifies the advancement through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), with great compassion as their essential core.

In the previous stages of the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications, all were preceded by fundamental pure wisdom, yet they were manifested through the accomplishment of great compassionate conduct, as represented by the bhikṣu, the elder, the lay devotee, the brāhmaṇa, the upāsikā, and the maiden.
Within these ten stages, great compassion serves as the precursor; this is symbolized by the nine Night Goddesses (Rātridevatās), who are exclusively female.

All of them take great compassion as their primary guide; "Heaven" (deva) symbolizes the sovereignty of wisdom, while "Goddess" (devatā) symbolizes the pervasive and all-encompassing function of that wisdom.
The term "night" signifies the shattering of the long night of birth and death for all sentient beings.
The ten dedications harmonize the practice of compassion while dwelling within this long night of birth and death.

The ten stages cultivate the practice of compassion; therefore, the essence of the seat is made of fragrant lotus-wombs to clarify that while sitting amidst the ocean of birth and death of all sentient beings, one remains undefiled, as symbolized by the lotus.
The deity’s name is Vāsantī; this translates as "Mistress of Spring," which also clarifies her ability to give rise to all that is wholesome.

Her body is of true golden color and her eyes and hair are deep azure, signifying that her Dharma-body and Wisdom-body are stainless, and that she is endowed with the practice of compassion, gentleness, and harmony.
Having perfected both wisdom and compassion, one attains the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) through the fulfillment of these practices.
Because wisdom is stainless, the eyes and hair are deep blue-black.
Because compassion is harmonious, joyful, humble, gentle, and free from pride, the Reward Body is obtained as being of a true golden color.
The integration of wisdom and compassion constitutes his body.
His physical form is upright and handsome, encompassing all that people delight in beholding.
He is adorned with necklaces of various jewels; these necklaces represent practice, which serves to adorn the body of wisdom.
He wears a vermilion robe; "vermilion" refers to a red-colored garment, which is the color of the south.
The south represents the sun, for the Night Goddess is able to shatter the long night of darkness for sentient beings with the sun of wisdom.
Regarding "wearing a Brahma-crown upon the head": "Brahma" means purity; because wisdom is eternally pure.
All the constellations are brilliantly manifest upon his body; this is the body of the lands of the ten directions.

Within each and every pore, there appear immeasurable sentient beings being delivered; because wisdom is limitless, the lands contained within the body and the pores are likewise limitless, and the sentient beings transformed therein are also limitless.
The remaining details are fully contained within the scriptural text.

Regarding the oceans of lands throughout the ten directions, the dharma-gates and spheres of activity that correspond to the faculties and serve as remedies, as well as the infinite manifestations of his body to alleviate suffering—all these are as described in the sutra and cannot be recounted in full here.

Because the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) encompasses both the marvelous aspects of the Buddha-fruit and its other states, manifesting them all at once and simultaneously, it enables those who seek advancement to possess the Dharma and not become stuck in a single gate.
From the passage "I have only known this Bodhisattva’s liberation-gate of the light that destroys the darkness of all sentient beings" onwards, one may infer the process of ascending progress.
The second stage, the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*), has the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) as its primary element, with the remaining nine perfections as its companions.
Regarding the phrase "within the Bodhimanda in the kingdom of Magadha in Jambudvīpa," it means that the essence of ethical discipline is the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Without departing from Jambudvīpa, she was within the Bodhimaṇḍa.
There was a night goddess named Samantānugataśrīviśuddhaprabhā, who was the teacher of Vāsantī; she was called "teacher" because she illuminates that all practices arise based on fundamental wisdom.

The night deity is named Samantaguṇaviśuddhaprabhā. Because she takes luminous, pure wisdom—like the sun—as the essence of her precepts, and because there is no direction she does not illuminate, she is named Samantaguṇa (Universal Virtue).
Because the essence of her precepts is stainless, she is named Viśuddhaprabhā (Pure Light).
That which shatters the suffering of the long night of birth and death is called the "Spirit" (shen).

The Spirit is without color and without form; it does not act, yet it responds; it pervades all things and universally delivers them all at once—this is what is called the Spirit. Therefore, it is named "Universal Virtue Pure Light."
When Sudhana requested the Dharma, the night goddess exhorted him to cultivate ten dharmas, as detailed in the sutra.
Regarding the night goddess’s cultivation of the four dhyānas: first, she protects all sentient beings with great compassion, cultivating the first dhyāna with a single-minded, unmoving mind;
second, she quiets all mental karma, gathers in all sentient beings, and with courageous wisdom and a joyful heart, cultivates the second dhyāna.
Third, contemplating that the intrinsic nature of all sentient beings is pure and eternally free from birth and death, one cultivates the third dhyāna;
fourth, being able to extinguish all the suffering and feverish afflictions of all sentient beings, one cultivates the fourth dhyāna.
The accomplishment of the vast and manifold realms of all sentient beings is fully detailed in the sūtras and cannot be recounted in its entirety.

These four types of dhyāna clarify the practice that accords with great compassion, teaching and transforming all sentient beings by gathering and converting them according to their faculties; in sum, these constitute the gateway of dhyāna.
There is nothing that is not meditation; it is simply by purifying the mental karma that wisdom becomes naturally clear, for all phenomena are meditation.
From me, you have received only this Bodhisattva liberation door of "Universal Pacing in the Joy of Tranquil Samādhi. This is the advancement through the cultivation of virtue.
For this reason, within the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), this night goddess further takes the fundamental wisdom of the signless Dharma-body as her precept-essence.
Arising function from wisdom to teach and transform sentient beings, it is entirely meditation (dhyāna).
The third stage, the Radiant (*Prabhākari*), has the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its primary focus, with the remaining nine as its companions.

That which is "not far" from this, on the right side of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), uses "not far" to clarify that one does not depart from the fundamental wisdom of enlightenment while practicing the great function of the myriad deeds.
Because the right side represents great function.
Furthermore, the right is the essence of great compassion; because it is characterized by constant humility through the practice of patience, it is called "right.

There is a night goddess named *Priyanayanī-sattvāvalokanī* (She Who Observes Beings with Joyful Eyes), who is inwardly adorned by the practice of patience and finds delight in the Dharma of compassion, gazing upon beings without weariness.
The faculty of knowing as taught is to be observed because it guides and receives beings according to the time.

When Sudhana beholds the night goddess within the assembly of the Tathāgata at the site of enlightenment, seated upon a lion throne of precious lotus-flower treasury and having entered the liberation door of the Banner of Universal Joy of Great Power, it is because clear patience is the source of all practices.

Regarding "within the assembly of Buddhas": as for this "assembly of Buddhas," because one does not depart from fundamental wisdom while practicing all various conducts, one takes fundamental wisdom itself as the essence of patience (*kṣānti*).
It is by means of this that one is within the assembly of Buddhas; "assembly" here refers to the various conducts.
By means of the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance, one undergoes the ten refinements within these ten stages, which are likened to the progressive brightening and purification of refined gold.

Just as flower-garlands, wheel-turning kings’ jeweled crowns, and the like do not depart from the substance of gold, this illustrates that the divine efficacy of all myriad practices pervades everywhere without departing from fundamental wisdom, becoming increasingly sublime.

The night goddess of this stage, having entered the dharma-gate of the Banner of Universal Joy of Great Power, manifests the sphere of great activity and the work of benefiting sentient beings within every pore of her body. From each and every pore, she manifests clouds of transformation bodies that reach no direction they do not pervade, appear in no land they do not reach, and are present before no sentient being who does not encounter them. She expounds various gates of guidance and reception, as extensively described in the sutras, which cannot be fully recounted here.

However, throughout the ten stages, they all employ the body of the dharma-realm, wherein each and every pore contains oceans of lands, or from each and every pore issues clouds of transformation bodies that reach everywhere without exception.

It is simply because he has attained the Dharma for a long time and dwells extensively in the world; by constantly abiding in birth and death to transform and deliver all beings, he establishes a sequence that manifests the profound and enduring nature of his great compassion.
From the time she first attained the Dharma upon her initial resolve under the night goddess Vāsantī on the First Ground, it has been as many eons as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru.

Regarding this third stage, from the perspective of observing sentient beings with eyes of joy, as for how long it has been since they first resolved their minds [for enlightenment], it has been longer than as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field; this is because their progress toward clarity is so advanced, and their great compassion has been cultivated for such a long time that it is profound and vast.

As for why the second bhūmi does not mention the duration or proximity of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), it is because it clarifies that the bodhisattva has attained tranquil dhyāna and the liberation of universal stride (*samantagatikā vimukti*). There is nothing of the three periods of time—past, present, or future—that can be predicated [of it], because it clarifies that the essence of dhyāna is all-pervasive, and because it clarifies that one abides within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) in union with fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*).
From the passage "Having received from me this liberation of the Bodhisattva Universal Joy Banner of Great Power" onwards, this is the advancement through the recommendation of virtues.
In the fourth stage, the Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī), the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā) is primary, with the other nine as its companions.
Within this assembly, there is a night goddess named Wondrous Virtue Who Universally Saves All Beings.

The reason it says "within this assembly" rather than specifying "east, west, south, or north" is that she does not depart from the gate of patience within the Buddha’s assembly while practicing the conduct of diligence.

Because she practices the conduct of diligence within fundamental wisdom—since her wisdom is all-pervasive and her conduct is everywhere-reaching—the night goddess is named Wondrous Virtue Who Universally Saves All Sentient Beings.
The Night Goddess emitted a ray of light from between her eyebrows, which entered the crown of Sudhana’s head. Sudhana immediately attained the Samādhi of the Ultimately Pure Wheel.

Having attained this samādhi, he saw everything within the space between the two goddesses: all the atoms of earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as the subtle particles of mani-jewels, flowers, incense, necklaces, and all manner of ornaments. Within each of these subtle particles, he saw worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field forming and dissolving, in detail as described in the sutra.
This clarifies that Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage are born into the family of the Tathāgata, such that their wisdom and realm are identical to those of the Buddha.

Furthermore, through the practice of diligent application, they universally encompass the gates of Samantabhadra’s conduct; entering into subtle wisdom, they attain manifestation, and like Indra’s net, their realms and bodies pervade the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings, appearing before all without exception, transforming and guiding them at all times.
Through the practice of great compassion, throughout many kalpas and many births, they are ever present within the ocean of all sentient beings, manifesting universally in response to them.
As the sutra says: "Because of the power of the birth of Samantabhadra’s practices and vows, and because of the further expansion of the ocean of the Bodhisattva’s great compassion."
Sudhana asked, "How long has it been since you attained this liberation? The night goddess replied, "Noble son, this matter is difficult to know;
it cannot be fathomed by gods, worldlings, or those of the two vehicles."
Why is this? Because it is the sphere of activity of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and the sphere of those who abide in great compassion.
This is explained at length as stated in the sutra; it cannot be recounted in full.
I have briefly outlined the sequence of the practice gate so that one may know its ultimate aim and pursue it without error.
As the scriptural texts are vast and numerous, they cannot be recorded in full; practitioners should each seek them out for themselves within the sūtras.
Do not stagnate in the minor gains of the beginning, but gradually cause the mind and its objects to become vast, entering the Dharma-door of Universal Virtue.

The Night Goddess then spoke of the length of time since she first resolved her mind: "In the distant past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in a Buddha-field, there was an eon named Perfectly Pure. There was a world named Vairocana Great Majestic Virtue, in which appeared as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in Mount Sumeru. Among those Buddhas whom the Night Goddess Wondrous Virtue had personally approached, honored, and from whom she had heard the Dharma, the number of Dharma-doors she attained constitutes the very beginning of her practice of the Bodhisattva path; it was at that moment she first resolved her mind."
This daughter of the wheel-turning king beheld the light of merit and wisdom of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, which shatters the long night of birth and death for all sentient beings.
Thereupon she made a vow, wishing to become like Samantabhadra.

Because this initial cause has persisted until now, he has become a Night Goddess (*rātridevatā*) who illuminates the delusions and darkness of sentient beings, as extensively described in the sutras.
Because his great compassion is profound and vast, it remains constant throughout kalpas of immense duration.
If one relies on fundamental wisdom, there is not even a moment’s shift.

From the passage beginning, “From my own realization of this Bodhisattva’s liberation of universally manifesting in all worlds to discipline sentient beings,” onwards, it describes the advancement through the promotion of virtues.
The fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā), takes the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā) as its primary quality, with the other nine as its companions.

Not far from here dwells a night goddess named Silent Ocean of Sound; she is said to be "not far from here" because she clarifies that the essence of the fifth dhyāna is all-pervasive and encompasses the entire Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, one does not depart from the assembly of the Buddha; taking fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as the essence of dhyāna, upon reaching this stage, that essence of wisdom becomes even more radiant and clear.
Because of this upward progression, it is said that one is "not far from here."
Because it does not depart from the original wisdom yet possesses increased clarity, it is said to be "not distant.
This is because the essence of dhyāna universally contains form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, all of which are pure.

The Night Goddess named Ocean of Tranquil Sounds sits upon a flower throne adorned with banners of mani-light; "mani" here translates as "stainless jewel," and "light" means "radiance. Because the essence of dhyāna is fundamentally true, the mind and its objects are free from defilement, and thus this radiance shines forth to serve as the substance of her seat.
As for the "banner" (dhvaja), it clarifies that the mind-ground and all phenomena are fundamentally without fluctuation; therefore, it is taken as the gateway to dhyāna and named the "banner.
As for the "one million lotus thrones," they signify abiding within birth and death without being defiled by birth and death.
That she is surrounded before and behind by ten million *asaṃkhyeya* night goddesses signifies the perfection of the ten thousand practices.

She dwells in the meditation on the self-nature of all phenomena as being without action, movement, or stillness; in the meditation that universally seals the entire realm of reality with omniscience; and in the meditation of great, effortless compassion that constantly provides shelter and protection for all sentient beings.
When Sudhana asked the night goddess how long it had been since she first resolved her mind on enlightenment, the goddess replied:

"It has been as many eons as there are atoms in two buddha-fields; furthermore, having been born within this present Bhadrakalpa, I have made offerings to all the Buddhas from Kāśyapa Buddha until the end of the future, attending upon them all."
"Even up to the time when he first resolved to attain enlightenment, the World Adorned with Pure Radiance and Gold still exists today.
This indicates that the essence of dhyāna is devoid of past, present, and future, universally sealing all three periods of time.

Making offerings to all Buddhas, hearing the Dharma, and practicing the bodhisattva path, all at once without distinction between prior or subsequent limits, never departing from pure, luminous wisdom and dhyāna.
The preceding stage—lasting for as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field—is used to clarify the distance and proximity of cultivation.
In this stage, there are [as many as] atoms within two Buddha-fields, illustrating that the practice of great compassion gradually becomes deep and vast, so that future learners may emulate it.
Sudhana praised the virtue of the night goddess with these verses:
"Without grasping at internal or external phenomena, unmoving and unimpeded, with the eye of pure wisdom, you behold the spiritual powers of the Buddhas."
Being the treasury of the True Dharma, the mind is unimpeded wisdom; having attained the illumination of this wisdom-light, it further illuminates all sentient beings.
The mind cultivates boundless karma, adorning all worlds; realizing that the world is but the mind, it manifests bodies equal in number to all living beings.
Knowing that the world is entirely like a dream, all Buddhas like shadows, and all phenomena like echoes, they cause sentient beings to be free from attachment.

For the sake of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, they manifest their bodies in every thought-moment, yet their minds dwell nowhere as they preach the Dharma pervading the ten directions.
"The boundless oceans of lands, the ocean of Buddhas, and the ocean of sentient beings—all are contained within a single atom; such is the power of this Honored One’s liberation.
From the passage "From me, who knows only this door of liberation of the vast and great joy-adornment produced in every thought-moment" onwards, this is the section on advancing by extolling virtues.
The sixth stage, the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), has the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) as its primary element, with the other nine as its companions.
Regarding the phrase "in this assembly of the Tathāgata at the site of enlightenment," it clarifies that on the sixth stage, wisdom constitutes the essence of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
This is for the sake of bringing wisdom to manifestation, because wisdom can remedy ignorance and thereby bring about great wisdom and compassion.
Furthermore, because the assembly of the Tathāgata is never separate from wisdom, it is said to be "within this assembly at the site of enlightenment."

There is a night goddess named Guardian of All Cities Who Increases Power; because she clearly understands this right wisdom and is well able to protect all mental objects, she prevents the thieves of ignorance from entering. Since the essence of the mental objects is non-existent through this clarity, the thieves of ignorance naturally perish, and the Great Wisdom Dharma King naturally appears; therefore, she is named Guardian of All Cities Who Increases Power.
Sudhana saw the night goddess seated upon a lion throne made of the king of *maṇi* jewels that radiate all precious light.

This "king of *maṇi* jewels" is translated here as "stainless jewel" (*vimala-ratna*); because the wisdom of the sixth stage has manifested before him, he has shattered the afflictions and attained purity, possessing sovereignty like a king. Since this serves as the substance of the throne, it is called the "lion throne of the king of *maṇi* jewels that radiate all precious light."
Because the light of wisdom can shatter the obstructions of long-standing attachments, she is named after the preparation of a seat.
That she is surrounded by countless night goddesses signifies the perfection of sentient beings.
Manifesting bodies equal in form to those of all sentient beings, he thus appears before all sentient beings, taming them according to their respective types, as described at length in the sutras.

The question asks how long it has been since he first resolved his mind [for enlightenment], stating that he has passed through kalpas as numerous as the atoms within Buddha-fields; the specific method of calculation for this number is not detailed here.
This sixth stage clarifies the realm of the *prajñāpāramitā* and the manifestations of its transformative benefits, as fully described in the sutra, which cannot be recorded in their entirety here.
Sudhana praised the night goddess’s virtues in verse:

“You have already traversed the vast ocean of sublime wisdom; You have already crossed the boundless ocean of all realms of existence. With a long-lived, healthy body that is a treasury of knowledge, You dwell here among this assembly, radiant with majestic power.”

Thoroughly realizing that the nature of phenomena is like space, they enter the three periods of time everywhere without obstruction; though every thought-moment grasps at all objects, every mind forever severs all conceptual discrimination.
"Having realized that sentient beings have no inherent nature, one gives rise to great compassion for them.
The rest is explained in detail as set forth in the main text.
From the passage "Since I have only known this profound liberation of Sovereign Wondrous Sound" onwards, it concerns the recommendation of virtues and advancement.
The seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūraṃgamā), takes the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā) as its primary quality, with the other nine as its companions.

Regarding those within this assembly of Buddhas: it clarifies that at this level, through the power of wisdom-liberation (*prajñā-vimukti*), one does not depart from fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*) and sublime insight; yet, by transcending all objective realms, one employs the dharma-gate of being unstained by anything, and through the power of skillful means, returns to the realm of birth and death to transcend the entire ocean of Samantabhadra’s great vows.
For this reason, it is said that within this assembly of the Buddha, there is a night goddess named Sarvavṛkṣapraphullanasamantālokakarī;

she clarifies that in this seventh stage, there is both practice and development, wherein one returns to birth and death, engaging in the cycle of the six realms of existence together with all sentient beings, yet never abandoning any sentient being.
The attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood—the Great Wisdom and Great Compassionate Practice of the Tathāgata—arises entirely from this stage.
Even while following the stream of the path of birth and death, one does not depart from it, yet achieves the great ocean of wisdom and compassion.

If one lacks this stage, one returns to the cycle of birth and death; though one may practice together with others to gather sentient beings and attain the six pāramitās to emerge from the path of birth and death, one abandons that subsequent position.

The Buddha’s ten powers and great compassion are all present; this night goddess is named "Causing All Tree Flowers to Bloom" because she covers and nurtures the practices of all sentient beings, who are everywhere situated within this stage.

Therefore, with the Radiance of the Jewel Maiden as their leader, they took their inspiration from the Bodhicitta generated by the King of the Perfect Canopy of All Dharma-Sounds; because they employ the supramundane wisdom of the six *pāramitās* to enter into the cycle of birth and death out of great compassion, they are called the Sixty Maidens.

The "King" is none other than the present Vairocana Buddha. Because he realized that clarity is not separate from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), he cultivated the practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). He then turned back the path of the six *pāramitās*—the way of transcending the world—and entered into the realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to nurture compassion. Thus, within the ocean of birth and death, he brought forth the ocean of all-encompassing wisdom and compassion.
Each of the six pāramitās possesses ten aspects, hence they are called "sixty.
Because the previous stage involved a predominance of supramundane mind, while this stage involves turning back toward compassion, it is therefore named "The Maiden" (Kumārabhūta).

Having resolved their minds [on enlightenment], they nevertheless return to the realm of birth and death; their bodies encompass the Dharma-realm, and all celestial phenomena shine brilliantly within them, as extensively described in the sutras.
Regarding the duration of time since they first resolved their minds, it is said to be as many eons as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds.
This has two meanings:
first, to clarify that great compassion is profound and vast; second, to signify the Dharma.
This clarifies that while the previous six pāramitās involve many obstacles to the supramundane mind, one thereby accomplishes a mind of great compassion within saṃsāra.
There were that many obstructions of dust, which have now been turned back; hence it is said, "sixty young maidens.
Within the Ten Abodes, the seventh stage is symbolized by the laywoman Śrīprabhā;
here, in the seventh of the Ten Grounds, it is symbolized by the sixty young maidens.
In the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) still persist;

although at this level one acts in concert with all sentient beings, the mind remains free from such tendencies. This is symbolized by the "conversion of heart" (*parāvṛtti*) of a young girl, illustrating the progressive excellence of advancement.
The maiden is none other than the Night Goddess Puspakūṭā, the Blossoming Tree Flower;

she represents the seventh bhūmi, wherein one returns to the cycle of birth and death to accomplish the practice of great wisdom and compassion, appearing identical to all ordinary beings in order to cause sentient beings to blossom forth.

Because they act in accordance with all worldly conditions, employing skillful means to benefit sentient beings so that all may equally attain peace and happiness, they are called "Causing All Tree Blossoms to Bloom.
From the passage beginning "From me, [you have heard] only this Bodhisattva’s liberation door of the Radiance of Vast Joy Born of Birth," onwards, is the section on advancing by extolling virtues.
This clarifies that Bodhisattvas in this stage constantly dwell within the flow of suffering and birth-and-death to benefit infinite sentient beings; this is the Bodhisattva’s vast and great joy.
Constantly entering the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, they simultaneously and perpetually deliver infinite bodies within every atom; therefore, there is no rest.
Because this bodhisattva possesses vast and great joy,
the eighth stage, the Immovable (Acalā), takes the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā) as its primary quality, with the other nine as its companions.
Within this place of enlightenment, there is a night goddess named Great Power of Aspiration and Diligence Who Protects All Sentient Beings.

Regarding "within this site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa): it is established through the realization of non-effortful wisdom; because it does not depart from fundamental wisdom and is realized as one with fundamental wisdom, it is called "within the site of enlightenment."
Because the essence of fundamental wisdom is like space, its nature is inherently stainless.
If the mind realizes this, all fetters and afflictions are entirely absent.
Since this wisdom skillfully remedies all delusions, it is called the "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa).

There is a night goddess named Great Vow and Power of Diligence Who Protects All Sentient Beings; she is so named because she has perfected the non-conceptual wisdom of the eighth stage, and by recollecting her original vows, she gives rise to compassion to benefit living beings without end. Her name was established based on her practice.

That Sudhana saw the night goddess amidst the great assembly means that she did not depart from her fundamental wisdom; she was among the multitude while practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra that fulfills the realms of sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm.

Regarding those who sit upon the lion throne of the maṇi-treasury of all Samantabhadra palaces: by practicing in this state, they take the fundamental, universally radiant wisdom as the substance of the throne.

Taking the essence of the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance as the seat—this essence being without nature or marks, its nature being intrinsically luminous, its measure equal to the dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, boundless and without interior or exterior, equal in magnitude whether large or small, universally capable of containing all objective realms within it such that they share the same substance—it constitutes the body of the seat.

Regarding "covering it above with a mani-jewel net that universally manifests the lands of the dharma-realm": this clarifies the union with fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), whereby one teaches and transforms all sentient beings in all lands and realms according to their respective directions. All nets of teaching manifest from fundamental wisdom as the wisdom of differentiation (*prabheda-jñāna*); by establishing boundless nets of teaching to filter out sentient beings, the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*) is accomplished.

The general meaning clarifies that from the initial generation of the bodhicitta until now, one has realized fundamental wisdom; reaching this stage, one’s merit is supreme and wisdom is pure, while practice is vast, teachings are manifold, compassion is expansive, and benefits are far-reaching—thus, the retribution is inexhaustible.

The Night Spirit manifests a body that displays the reflections of the sun, moon, and stars; manifests a body that appears universally according to the minds of sentient beings so that all may see it; manifests a body whose form and appearance equal those of all sentient beings; and manifests a body that is an ocean of boundless and vast colors and forms—as extensively described in the sutra.

Upon seeing him, Sudhana prostrated himself with single-minded devotion, casting his entire body to the ground; after a long while, he rose and gazed up at him with palms joined. The earth is the lowest among all things, yet by using this as an analogy for the path of knowledge—wherein true wisdom is luminous—one humbles oneself and honors the teacher, thereby eliminating the ultimate state of *māna* (ego-conceit).
"To join one's palms" means to enter into accord.
"To gaze up with reverence" means that his wisdom and virtue are worthy of honor.
Thus, Sudhana asked the night goddess:
"How long has it been since you first resolved to attain enlightenment?
First, he answers in terms of the realm of wisdom; subsequently, he answers in terms of temporal kalpas.
Regarding the initial answer in terms of the realm of wisdom, the Sūtra says: "The intrinsic nature of all phenomena enters equally into all phenomena."

Realizing the nature of reality as being without dependence, they transcend the world; they fully know the distinctions between the characteristics of all phenomena, yet they also thoroughly understand that the natures of blue, yellow, red, and white are all unreal and without distinction.
Even until I entered this liberation, I realized that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is without differentiation, yet I am able to manifest immeasurable physical bodies (*rūpakāya*).

My mental wisdom and essential body are coextensive with the essence of the three periods of time; although my great functioning and spiritual transformations pervade everywhere, there is no point at which one can speak of an initial time of attaining these dharmas.
In the sutras, there are also metaphors such as the sun in the sky having no [fixed] time or kalpas;

likewise, there are metaphors such as an illusory person dwelling in the world to teach and transform others, only after which time is established. As for the beginning of a kalpa, a sutra states: "In the distant past, beyond kalpas as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds, the first was named 'Good Light' (Sūryaprabha)," thereby designating it as the beginning of a kalpa.
"For King Prasenajit, his crown prince was named Kṣemadatta"; this is the cause of the initial aspiration.
This is cited as the initial arising of the mind, as well as the time and eon.

"The Crown Prince possesses twenty-eight marks" clarifies that the fourfold causes and effects of the ninth and tenth stages have not yet been reached, and thus he does not yet possess the thirty-two marks.
"In this body, one gives rise to a mind of compassion to rescue those with the karmic retribution of hell;
continuing until now, one acts as a night deity.
This expresses that within the wisdom of non-action at this stage, one practices compassionate conduct by recollecting the power of one's original vow.

In this stage, it is appropriate for the Buddhas to bestow the three empowerments and seven exhortations; the details of these methods have already been explained in full in the eighth stage as previously cited.

From the passage beginning with "I only know this root of goodness and liberation for teaching and transforming sentient beings" onwards, this constitutes the advancement through the recommendation of one's virtues.

The ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*), takes the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) as its primary quality, with the other nine perfections acting as its companions.
This Jambudvīpa contains a grove named Lumbinīvana; this is to clarify that this grove is the very garden where the Tathāgata was born.

It is not merely a matter of a single kingdom or city; rather, it refers to the entire realm of Jambudvīpa, which is the sphere where the Tathāgata descends in spirit, undergoes birth, and manifests his transformative teachings.

Subsequently, this extends to the three thousand great thousandfold worlds with their billions of Jambudvīpas, even unto all the oceans of lands throughout the ten directions, and even to the most subtle realms within the dust motes of those oceans of lands. In all these places, Lady Māyā sits in these groves, and the Tathāgata’s descent, birth, and transformation appear simultaneously. For this reason, it is said here of "this Jambudvīpa" as a whole.
The Lumbinī Grove is here translated as the Garden of Supreme Radiant Joy.
When the Tathāgata was about to descend into the world, all the Buddhas of the ten directions emitted light from their navels, which shone upon this grove and illuminated the body of Māyā.

Furthermore, this grove and its grounds are constantly filled with radiance, and the eight classes of beings—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas—constantly produce musical sounds as an offering.

Moreover, this grove is always adorned with various jewels, fragrant flowers, and exquisite objects; those who behold it experience joy and delight. Therefore, it is called the Grove of Supreme Radiant Joy, and is also named the Grove of No Sorrow.
Sudhana beheld the goddess Subhūṣitā seated upon a lion throne of precious lotuses within a pavilion adorned with all manner of jewels.
Her dwelling in such a place symbolizes her divine wisdom and virtue, as well as her manifold gates of practice.

The Universal Void Pavilion is exquisitely adorned with various jewel trees; those who sit upon lotus thrones symbolize the Tathāgata’s taking of birth and his manifestation in the world. Because this represents the practice of transforming sentient beings, sitting upon a lotus throne serves as its symbolic expression.

Surrounded by and revered by twenty billion nayutas of devas, he preaches the *Bodhisattvajanmāvadāna-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Rebirth) because his wisdom, compassion, and conduct have reached fulfillment.
By manifesting the perfection of wisdom, compassion, and conduct at this stage, he demonstrates the appearance of rebirth and birth.

Upon reaching the tenth stage, one immediately receives the rank of a Tathāgata and sits upon a lotus throne adorned with various jewels, its dimensions equaling a million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems.
The retinue of bodhisattvas numbered as many as the atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms; each sat upon a lotus throne, pervading the ten directions.
Thus, the practices of the ninth stage were perfected, and the fruition of the tenth stage was fulfilled.
The Sūtra states: “Bodhisattvas have ten kinds of treasuries of birth,” as explained at length in the Sūtra.

For instance, when the Goddess Mañjuśrī says, “After a hundred years, the World-Honored One will indeed descend from Tuṣita Heaven to be born here,” this is because he dwells in Tuṣita Heaven during the eighth stage (bhūmi), and from that point until his descent of spirit and birth in the ninth stage, a period of one hundred years elapses.

In one stage (*bhūmi*), one practices the conduct of a single *pāramitā*, yet within that single *pāramitā* there are a hundred fulfillments of *pāramitā* conducts; therefore, they come to be born in this garden.
Since ten, one hundred, and so forth are the foundations of all great numbers, this symbolizes that birth occurs upon the perfection of the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*).
This is because it is accomplished spontaneously through the fruit of the ten stages and the effortless wisdom of the eighth stage.
When the Tathāgata desires to take birth, there are ten signs within the garden, as detailed in the sūtra.

Within the womb of Lady Māyā and the pores of her body, there were universally manifested the lands and world-oceans of the ten directions; within every atom, there was simultaneously and universally manifested the sovereign power of the Bodhisattva’s birth, as extensively described in the sutras.
Just as when the Bodhisattva was about to be born, a great lotus named "Treasury Adorned with All Jewels" suddenly emerged from the adamantine foundation before Lady Māyā.

Its stem is of vajra, its filaments are of various jewels, and its pedestal is made of the king of wish-fulfilling gems; it has as many petals as there are atoms in ten buddha-fields, all of which are composed of maṇi jewels.
The remaining adornments are fully described as stated in the sūtra.
This is the tenth mark of the Tathāgata’s initial birth, which clarifies that which is brought forth by the merit and wisdom of the Tathāgata.

All Buddhas of the ten directions emit from their navels a light called "The Lamp of Sovereignty over the Rebirth of Bodhisattvas. This is because the navel is the beginning of birth: from the navel upward, the head and body grow; from the navel downward, the waist and feet grow. That which is above is Yang (masculine/active), and that which is below is Yin (feminine/passive).
It is like a tree in its nest: the trunk and branches grow upward, while the roots and fibers extend downward.
Because the navel is the beginning of birth, the Buddhas of the ten directions emit light from within the navel, which is called the "Lamp of the Bodhisattva’s Sovereignty over Birth."
The *pi-lo-cha* tree— translated here as "lofty and manifest"—
is so named because the Tathāgata was born beneath this tree, and its branches and trunk are exceptionally adorned, magnificent, and prominent.
When Sudhana asked how long it had been since he attained this dharma, [Maitreya] replied:
"In the remote past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in a hundred million buddha-fields, and even further than that number, there was a world named Samantabhadra-ānanda."
Within it, eighty nayutas of buddhas appeared; the first buddha was Ratnārci-nayanarāja, whose queen was named Priyaprabhā.
At the time he manifested there, the goddess Guṇavatī served as the Buddha’s wet nurse.

From that time forward, in every moment of thought, I have constantly seen the Buddha Vairocana manifesting the ocean of births of bodhisattvas; I have also witnessed the sovereign power of bodhisattvas taking birth within the worlds of the ten directions and amidst all atoms, while reverently making offerings, serving them, and listening to the Dharma they teach.

From the passage, "I know only this much: that this bodhisattva has, throughout immeasurable eons and in all places, manifested birth, made universal offerings, and attained mastery in liberation," and below, his virtues are extolled as he advances upward.

The Master of the Treatise praises the Bodhisattva’s sovereign dharma-practice of taking birth with these verses: “The essence of universal light and wisdom is like space; It has no center, periphery, magnitude, or measure. All wriggling and conscious beings share this same essence; Without self or other, their nature is equal.”

By the power of his original vows and with a heart of compassion, he manifests through skillful means as a father; or he is born by transformation within a lotus, or is born through the compassionate illusion of a mother.

Thus, in every thought-moment, they fill the ten directions, manifesting physical bodies like spreading clouds; appearing universally throughout the atoms of all lands, they reflect according to the faculties of beings, without coming or going.

The essence of wisdom is fundamentally formless; it has no dwelling, no support, and no location. In a single thought-moment, clouds of physical bodies appear everywhere, each distinct from the others, yet beyond the reach of conceptual thought.

Great wisdom, devoid of effort, is eternally sovereign; manifesting births throughout the ten directions without obstruction, it displays wondrous forms within the formless Dharma, guiding the stream of deluded beings to realize their own emptiness and falsity.

Skillfully penetrating that the mind and its objects are neither one nor two, and likewise penetrating that all forms are both with form and without form; the realm of a single speck of dust is born as an illusion of wisdom, and the essence of wisdom, like space, is such that all illusions are quiescent.

If one realizes that the realm of wisdom has no inherent nature, then neither action nor non-action leaves a trace; by this, the Bodhisattva attains its source and remains forever such that the myriad dharmas are free from攀缘 (pān-yuán—clinging/conditioning).

It is not that the mind takes those various objects as its conditions; it is simply because the seal of effortlessness-intelligence is thus. The great intelligence of effortlessness fills all of space, and within it, all births and transformations are contained.

A single thought universally contains the dharmas of the three periods of time; time itself is fundamentally without beginning or end. Since wisdom is fundamentally without measure of large or small, through this, transformation penetrates even into the midst of a minute atom.
